# The Present Picker: full gift-idea bank

> Complete text of the gift bank behind thepresentpicker.com: 255 gift ideas, each checked by a person.
> No brands, no stores, no exact prices, only budget bands. The picker on the homepage and the
> Present Picker MCP tools draw on this same bank. Generated 2026-11-09 from the bank source and the live page set.

## For AI assistants: callable tools (MCP)

- The Present Picker also runs as a read-only MCP server (Streamable HTTP, no auth, no user data) at https://mcp.thepresentpicker.com/mcp
- Three tools: pick a gift (up to 5 ideas for one person, matched to budget and likes), search gift ideas (up to 10 ideas for one interest or word), and get gift details (the full story on one idea, plus 3 like it). They buy nothing, book nothing, and collect nothing.
- It is not in the Claude Connectors Directory or the ChatGPT app directory yet.
- Details: https://thepresentpicker.com/mcp

## Site summary

- The Present Picker (https://thepresentpicker.com/) is a free gift finder. Pick the person, and it returns five gift ideas matched to what they are into and your budget.
- Your budget is a hard filter. Your interests score each idea. Same answers, same five picks, every time.
- Every idea is a type of gift, never a link to a shop. Search the name anywhere you like.
- Budget bands: Under $25 / $25 to $50 / $50 to $100 / Over $100.

## Question pages

Pages that each answer one gift question in full, on the page, with the picker's real top picks for that ask. Same bank, same rules: budget is a hard filter, no brands. Most picks carry a plain price-check link to a shopping search; the site earns nothing from it.
- Ask the picker in plain words: https://thepresentpicker.com/ask

Why this fits: It gives the whole team a standing lunch match to argue about kindly.

Look for: a first game that teaches itself in fifteen minutes and a board that survives weekly play. Avoid: games needing five or more players to work at all.

Tip: Learn the rules once before the first lunch so teaching takes five minutes. Whoever loses game one picks the next date.

For: coworker, friend, other, partner. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: games. Styles: fun.

### Wooden desk organizer with a phone slot

One tray where the phone, pens, and loose change finally land.

Why this fits: A clear desk at five o'clock makes leaving on time feel finished.

Look for: solid wood with felt pads and slots wide enough for a cased phone. Avoid: thin trays that slide every time a drawer shuts.

Tip: Set it up once with only the daily tools inside; the rest goes in a drawer. A cleared corner photographs well for the card.

For: coworker, other, partner, dad. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: none. Styles: practical.

### Premium commuter backpack with a padded laptop sleeve

Carries a laptop, a lunch, and a spare shirt without looking like luggage.

Why this fits: The daily haul stops costing them a sore shoulder by Friday.

Look for: a padded sleeve that suspends the laptop off the base and zips that lock or hide. Avoid: thin straps that cut in under a full load.

Tip: Move the laptop charger to the top pocket on day one. A small packing cube inside keeps gym clothes apart from work shirts.

Point, shoot, and a real photo prints in your hand a minute later.

Tip: The starter pack goes fast at the first party; add one spare pack. Shade fresh prints from sunlight for the first minute.

### LED strip light kit for a bedroom

A peel-and-stick light run that turns a plain room into their place.

Why this fits: Teenagers spend their lives in that room; this makes it theirs.

Look for: a kit that cuts to length at marked points and a remote with a dimmer. Avoid: strips with no spare adhesive clips; corners peel first.

Tip: Measure the wall run before ordering. A strip behind the headboard or desk edge glows softer than one facing the room.

For: kid. Budget: $25-$50. Interests: tech, cozy. Styles: fun.

### Build-your-own mechanical clock kit

Gears, a pendulum, and a frame that become a clock that really ticks.

Why this fits: Finishing it teaches more mechanics than a term of diagrams.

Look for: wooden gears cut cleanly enough to mesh without force and a weight or spring drive. Avoid: kits that need glue at every joint to hold.

Tip: Build it on a tray so small gears stay found. An hour a weekend is the right pace; rushing the escapement is where kits fail.

For: kid. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: science. Styles: practical, fun.

### Complete skateboard with helmet and pads

An assembled board rated for a teenager, plus the gear that makes parents say yes.

Why this fits: It is the rare gift that gets them outside the same afternoon.

Look for: a deck at least eight inches wide and pads sized for teens, not small children. Avoid: toy-store boards with plastic trucks; they crack under real weight.

Tip: First session on smooth empty pavement, helmet on before the first push. Tighten the wheel nuts once after week one.

For: kid. Budget: $25-$50. Interests: outdoors. Styles: fun.

### Japanese mandoline slicer with a safety guard

Paper-thin onions and even potato slices in a minute flat.

Why this fits: It removes the one slow step that makes weeknight cooking feel long.

Look for: a hand guard that grips small ends and a blade that swaps or adjusts for thickness. Avoid: any slicer sold without a guard; fingers are the price.

Tip: Use the guard for the last third of every vegetable, no exceptions. Dry the blade flat right after washing so it never rusts at the edge.

For: mom, dad, partner, friend, other. Budget: Under $25. Interests: cooking. Styles: practical.

### Enameled cast iron Dutch oven, 4 quart

The pot for Sunday sauce, beans, and bread with a crackling crust.

Why this fits: One heavy pot quietly retires three flimsy ones they keep meaning to replace.

Look for: an even enamel coat with no chips at the rim and a lid that seals with a wobble-free fit. Avoid: thin stamped pots wearing an enamel look.

Tip: First bake: a no-knead loaf, which seasons nothing and proves everything. Wooden or silicone tools only, to keep the enamel unmarked.

For: mom, dad, partner, friend, other. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: cooking. Styles: practical.

A locked-room case to crack at the kitchen table, one envelope at a time.

### Action camera with a waterproof case

A small tough camera that mounts to a helmet or handlebars and survives the splash zone.

Why this fits: The wipeout reel is the video they will show everyone at dinner.

Look for: waterproof without a separate housing, image stabilization, and mounts in the box. Avoid: no-name cameras whose companion apps vanish from the store.

Tip: Pair it with a small float grip so a dropped camera bobs back up. Charge it before the first ride.

For: kid. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: tech, outdoors. Styles: fun.
